reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / DeVita's Cancer: Principles & Practice of Oncology
clinicalPearls: It is a subacute inflammatory lung injury that typically develops weeks to a few months after thoracic radiotherapy, most often for lung, breast, oesophageal, or mediastinal tumours
Presenting features include dry cough, exertional breathlessness, low-grade fever, and sometimes pleuritic chest pain, which can mimic infection or cancer progression
Risk is influenced by the volume of lung irradiated, total dose and fractionation, pre-existing lung disease, and concurrent or prior chemotherapy or immunotherapy
Imaging classically shows ground-glass or consolidative change corresponding to the radiation field, though the distribution may extend beyond classic field borders with modern conformal techniques
It is fundamentally a diagnosis of exclusion, requiring careful exclusion of infection, pulmonary embolism, lymphangitic tumour spread, and drug-induced pneumonitis
Mild cases may be managed with observation and supportive care, while symptomatic disease is treated principally with corticosteroids and gradual tapering
Concurrent immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy can potentiate or complicate lung toxicity, making the distinction from immune-related pneumonitis important
Untreated or severe pneumonitis can progress over months to irreversible radiation-induced pulmonary fibrosis
reference.pathophysiology: Ionising radiation damages alveolar epithelial and vascular endothelial cells within the treated lung volume, triggering release of inflammatory cytokines and reactive oxygen species. This produces an acute to subacute alveolitis with increased capillary permeability, protein-rich exudate, and impaired gas exchange, seen clinically as radiation pneumonitis. If inflammation and fibroblast activation persist, the process evolves into progressive collagen deposition and radiation fibrosis with permanent architectural distortion and volume loss. The severity relates to the dose delivered and the volume of normal lung exposed, modified by patient and treatment factors.
additionalDifferentials: Lymphangitic carcinomatosis or tumour progression in the lung
Drug-induced or immune checkpoint inhibitor pneumonitis
Exacerbation of underlying interstitial lung disease
additionalInvestigations: Chest radiograph and high-resolution CT correlating changes with the radiation field
Oxygen saturation and, where indicated, arterial blood gas and lung function testing
Inflammatory markers and cultures to help exclude infection
Bronchoscopy with lavage in selected cases to exclude infection or alternative diagnoses
Review of the radiotherapy plan and concurrent systemic therapy including immunotherapy
redFlags: High fever or purulent sputum suggesting superimposed infection
Extensive bilateral changes extending beyond the radiation field
Progression toward respiratory failure despite corticosteroid therapy
reference.prognosis: Most mild to moderate cases respond well to corticosteroids and resolve, but severe pneumonitis, extensive lung involvement, or progression to fibrosis can cause lasting respiratory impairment and, uncommonly, death.
pitfalls: Assuming symptoms represent infection and delaying appropriate anti-inflammatory treatment
Missing tumour progression or pulmonary embolism by anchoring on radiation pneumonitis
Tapering corticosteroids too rapidly and provoking a symptom flare
Failing to consider concurrent immune-related pneumonitis in patients on checkpoint inhibitors
references: DeVita's Cancer: Principles & Practice of Oncology
management: Corticosteroids with a gradual taper as the mainstay for symptomatic pneumonitis, reserving observation and supportive care for mild disease
Supplemental oxygen and symptomatic measures such as antitussives for breathlessness and cough
Exclusion and treatment of infection, pulmonary embolism and tumour progression before attributing symptoms to pneumonitis
Steroid-sparing immunosuppression for corticosteroid-refractory or immunotherapy-associated cases
Monitoring of oxygenation and lung function with vigilance for progression to radiation fibrosis
Review of the radiotherapy plan and concurrent systemic therapy, coordinated between clinical oncology and respiratory medicine
